topic: Thrinaxodon and Broomistega -- predator and injured amphibian shared a burrow, fossilized together by a flash flood
title: A Predator Shared Its Den With Injured Prey -- 250M-Year-Old Proof
description: AI-narrated original commentary on a real 2013 paleontology discovery: a 250-million-year-old Karoo Basin burrow where a mammal ancestor (Thrinaxodon) and an injured amphibian (Broomistega) sheltered side by side, revealed by synchrotron CT scanning. Not a repost -- original script and voice.

hook_candidates.text: A badly injured amphibian crawled into a predator's den -- and the predator let it stay.
A 250-million-year-old fossil shows a predator and its injured prey sharing the same den, untouched.
Why didn't a meat-eating mammal ancestor kill the injured amphibian sleeping right next to it?
Finding a predator fossilized next to its prey doesn't always mean it killed it.

payoff_mechanism: Thrinaxodon was aestivating, a dormant near-hibernation state that shuts down an animal's activity and metabolism to survive drought, which meant its predatory instincts were switched off and it never reacted to the injured amphibian sharing its den.
share_trigger: A viewer sends this to the friend who's obsessed with true crime documentaries, because they want to show them a 250-million-year-old case that isn't actually a murder.
contradicted_belief: People assume finding a predator fossilized right next to its prey means the predator attacked and killed it.

beats.text: A badly injured amphibian crawled into a predator's den -- and the predator let it **stay**.
250 million years ago in South Africa, an amphibian called Broomistega -- with **seven** broken ribs -- crawled into a predator's burrow.

The predator, Thrinaxodon, wasn't awake to attack -- it was **aestivating**, a dormant state animals used to survive brutal drought after Earth's worst mass extinction, so its hunting instinct never switched on.
Scientists found this in 2013, using a **synchrotron** -- an X-ray strong enough to see inside solid rock.
That shelter held for weeks -- until a flash **flood** buried both animals together, exactly as they were found. Follow for the next one science almost missed.
